rounds.name: Technical Interview Round 1
rounds.description: I started by introducing myself. They immediately dived deep into my projects, which I had prepared for. Then they gave me the Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock II problem. I already knew it from Striver’s DP sheet, so I explained the DP approach confidently. They then asked for the O(n) linear approach — I explained but made a small mistake. They kindly corrected me and said, “You’re on the right track.” That encouragement boosted my confidence mid-interview. They also asked me about the difference between React and normal HTML/CSS and some questions related to my resume . Then came a rapid-fire round: factorial (loop & recursion), recursion issues (I said TLE), which DS recursion uses (Stack), why use DP, assigning priority to objects (I said priority queue). I liked this part because it felt like a fun quiz rather than grilling. Some other candidates were asked to open Google Colab do some visualizations/operations on dataset; I wasn’t asked that. Overall, my interview went well.

rounds.name: Technical Interview Round 2
rounds.description: We started again with a quick intro and discussion of one of my hackathon projects. Then they gave me a case study: “You’re a Senior Data Analyst at AuxoAI. Microsoft needs 1000 applicants for a job. You have job seeker data from your client. How would you select 1000 candidates for that job role?” I gave some thought then I said I’d parse resumes using pyresparser and extract features like skills, education, location, and experience, and a few more features that I don’t clearly remember now.. My output would be “Eligible/Not Eligible.” I initially said Naive Bayes for the model. Then they asked how I’d handle candidates backing out at the last moment. At first, I overcomplicated it — I said I would check factors like college tier (if someone is from a top college, they might get better offers), location preferences, salary expectations, and experience level. I thought of approaching it with regression, reasoning that more experienced candidates usually want better opportunities. But they immediately pointed out that this is actually a classification problem. At that moment, I realized my mistake, smiled, and corrected myself: “In that case, I will use Logistic Regression to classify whether a candidate is likely to back out or not.” I felt like I redeemed myself here by being honest and flexible. Other candidates were asked guesstimates — so be ready for that too.

rounds.name: Technical Round 1
rounds.description: I introduced myself to the panel and then they asked me to select a project on which a deep dive could be possible . I chose the first project on my resume(It was a LSTM+ XGBOOST hybrid model ) , where I explained in detail the methodology of the project .They proceeded by asking the information about the columns used and why only those were selected, the source of the data , the number of rows present , and related questions. They then asked me to tell the metrics of the model (R2_SCORE and the MSE error) and inquired about the mathematical formulas of the metrics and the intuition behind them.(Some questions such as “explain R2_score to a layman” were also asked. Then I was asked in detail (bohot depth me gaye) about XGBOOST and LSTM and the mathematical intuition behind them .I answered almost all the questions correctly and they were pleased with my fundamentals.They asked me about the gradient descent algorithm and how it works and its mathematical intricacies(fundamental understanding of coordinate geometry and curves is needed). Finally I was asked a bit about GEN-AI . To wrap up the interview , I was asked a simple DSA question.( Sieve of Eratosthenes) . The expectation was to write a working code . I explained the brute force solution and then explained in detail the optimal approach . I coded the solution (easy tha) and they were pleased by it(it seemed) .Next I was asked about the TC and the SC of the solution ,and I correctly answered it. The interview concluded with me asking a question to the panel . The round lasted around 40 minutes.

tips.text: Since this is an AIML role, I would suggest that you should have all the projects in the field of AIML. Please try not to include development projects (if possible).

I would recommend including 1–2 projects on your resume where you have developed machine learning models from scratch. These projects highlight your ability to code from scratch and demonstrate a strong fundamental understanding of concepts.
Work experience is always appreciated. Try to have an internship before the placement season starts.
Try to have C++ or Python as your primary language and then study OOPS in Java for a well-rounded knowledge base.

The aptitude section for AuxoAI was of a moderate to high difficulty level .I personally used my strong intuition of mathematics to solve the questions.While I had all the time in the world to solve the questions , it won’t always be the same .I solved 18-19 questions .
Have strong fundamentals of machine learning and mathematics.
Be calm.
In the guesstimate, I did all the calculations mentally , rather than on paper. This can help you . Also it is important to break the problem statement into smaller parts and then find the solution.
A calm mind is the need of the hour .You might be put in unknown and extreme high pressure situations throughout the whole placement process and it is important to not lose your sense of reasoning .
Prepare answers for standard HR questions beforehand (jot down the main points) and then try to relate all these points to weave a story .
Have a strong group of people around you who genuinely wish for your success.
Believe in God’s plan.
it is fine to take a break of 1-2 days after a rejection and then have a fresh start leaving everything behind .
Patience is something which is quite underrated in this journey. While people around you might be in a hurry to get placed, it is important to keep calm, think rationally, and then take any decision.

Luck and the importance of timing cannot be understated in this journey. While consistently getting the toughest questions in OAs (randomized questions in OA) broke me , I was really lucky that AuxoAI came for hiring. Luck evens out in the end (law of averages) but for luck to be on your side, you should be ready to work really hard even in adversity.

rounds.name: Online Assesment Round
rounds.description: The online assessment round was conducted on the HackerRank platform. It consisted of 36 questions to be solved in 120 minutes, covering topics from Computer Networking, Operating Systems, SQL, Logical Reasoning, Probability, and Puzzles, along with two DSA questions based on sliding windows and trees. The sliding window problem was easy, while the tree problem was of medium difficulty. There were also multiple SQL query-based questions that tested the basics of joins, aggregate functions, and constraints. The non-technical questions focused on aptitude and logical reasoning, which included probability-based problems and short analytical puzzles. We had to take the test from home due to heavy rainfall, which made it impossible to conduct the online assessment on campus that day.

rounds.name: Technical Interview I
rounds.description: The interviews began soon after the pre-placement talk ended at around 12:00 p.m. I was allotted to Panel 1, and I was the second candidate from my panel to be interviewed. As soon as I entered the room, the interviewer greeted me, offered me a seat, and asked me to introduce myself. After my introduction, he went through my resume and asked about the first project mentioned in it. He then questioned some of my technical choices, such as why I used JavaScript for the project, why I didn’t use Next.js, and how I would convince him to use React instead of Next.js. Since I had used a Sentence Transformer model in my project, he asked me whether I was familiar with NLP. I told him that NLP is one of my core subjects this semester. His focus then shifted to NLP-related questions. Then his focus shifted to DSA, and he gave me a question on valid anagrams to solve. I wrote the pseudocode for it on paper, and the interviewer seemed quietly satisfied with my approach. After that, he asked me to write code to sort a string, which I implemented using bubble sort. Next, the discussion moved to DBMS and SQL. He also questioned me about candidate keys, primary keys, and foreign keys. Since I had mentioned MongoDB in my technical section, he asked me how to fetch the second-highest salary using MongoDB. After that, he moved to OOPs concepts and asked me to elaborate on the four pillars of OOPs with real-life examples. As my primary programming language is C++, he still asked whether multiple inheritance is supported in Java, along with some basic questions on memory management in Java. He then shifted to React, asking about Hooks, followed by some basic questions on Postman, Thunder Client, Git, and GitHub. At the end of the interview, he asked if I had any questions for him. I inquired about the type of work involved in the role and the training process. The entire round lasted for about 40–45 minutes.

rounds.name: Technical-Interview II
rounds.description: For this round, I was the second candidate in my panel to be interviewed. This round was purely focused on databases and lasted for around 50–55 minutes. All the questions were based on SQL, MongoDB, and Database Management Systems (DBMS). The interviewer first asked me to introduce myself, and then, similar to the first round, he asked me to explain my first project. He also asked me to design the schema of my project on paper. While designing, I explained my approach, discussed how I chose the primary keys, the cardinalities, and the relationships between tables. After that, he asked me to write several SQL queries—around 7 to 8 in total—and I was able to solve all of them. There were also some output prediction questions. He asked me the difference between DROP, TRUNCATE, and DELETE commands, and in which scenarios DELETE is used. I explained that DELETE is used with the WHERE condition. Then he gave me the query DELETE FROM table; and asked whether it would work without a WHERE condition. I answered that it would work, but it would be slower than DROP since it deletes the rows one by one. Next, he asked about ACID properties, deadlocks, and the types of SQL commands. I mentioned DDL, DML, DCL, and TCL. He then asked me to elaborate on TCL commands, and I explained COMMIT, ROLLBACK, and SAVEPOINT. He also asked a scenario-based question related to SAVEPOINT, which I was not completely sure about, so I politely told him that I was not very familiar with that concept. Then he moved on to ask the difference between functions and procedures, gave me a query to write a trigger, and followed up with multiple questions on views, joins, aggregate functions, procedures, UNION, and UNION ALL. He also asked about cursors in databases—which I honestly didn’t know—and several questions on indexing, including the difference between clustered and non-clustered indexes, and whether indexing would be effective for a table with millions of rows, along with a few scenario-based questions.

tips.text: It is not necessary to give the correct answer to every question the interviewer asks. The key is to stay confident throughout.

If you don’t know the answer to a question, avoid directly saying “I don’t know.” Instead, try to relate the question to some relevant concepts and explain your thought process. If the interviewer is still not satisfied, you can politely say, “I’m not completely sure about this, but I’ll definitely look into it.”
I strongly suggest maintaining a good CGPA throughout your academics. Try to keep it above 7.5, but to maximize your chances of getting shortlisted by most companies, aim for a CGPA of 8 or higher.
So, along with DSA, make sure to practice aptitude questions regularly.
